item.title: IBM's Granite 4.1 LLMON previews train the model to separate instructions from data, claiming near-zero indirect prompt-injection success. What security teams should test
item.description: Reserved special tokens that user content cannot forge, and unique IDs that bind each instruction to the data it may act on: it is the first vendor attempt to make injection resistance a property of the model rather than of the prompt.
item.content:encoded:
Reserved special tokens that user content cannot forge, and unique IDs that bind each instruction to the data it may act on: it is the first vendor attempt to make injection resistance a property of the model rather than of the prompt.

Prompt injection has resisted every fix because the model cannot tell where the instruction ends and the data begins. A system prompt says 'treat the following as data'; a retrieved web page says 'ignore the above'; both are text, and the model weighs them the same way. On Wednesday IBM published two experimental models, granite-4.1-3b-llmon-preview and granite-4.1-8b-llmon-preview, trained on a format designed to remove that ambiguity, and reported results that would matter a great deal if they hold up.

What LLMON is

LLM Object Notation, pronounced 'lemon', is an XML-like markup for prompts. Two features do the work. First, the structural delimiters are reserved special tokens in the vocabulary, not ordinary characters, so nothing in user or retrieved content can produce an opening or closing tag; the classic injection trick of mimicking a system marker is impossible at the tokeniser level. Second, tags carry semantic roles, instructions, data, requirements, and unique IDs bind each instruction to the specific data it is allowed to act on, in the way a function's arguments are bound to its parameters. Content that is not referenced by the execution block is meant to be ignored. Existing JSON converts to LLMON and back without loss, and IBM says the format complements chat templates rather than replacing them.

The numbers

On OPI, a benchmark of indirect prompt injections hidden in retrieved content, IBM reports that attack success for the LLMON models drops to nearly zero, while the non-LLMON baselines it tested remain highly susceptible. Expressed as robustness, the LLMON models avoid 47% more attacks than the best frontier model IBM tested and 95% more than the best open-source model. Similar trends are reported on the ASB and StruQ benchmarks. On standard capability benchmarks the previews perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models, so the resistance does not appear to cost utility. The exact per-model figures are in charts rather than text, and IBM has not named the frontier model it compared against.

The caveats IBM states

This is an experimental preview for evaluation, not production. The injection resistance is 'a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee': the model has been trained to ignore unreferenced instructions, but nothing in the architecture prevents it from obeying one. The benchmarks cover static indirect injections; adaptive attacks that unfold over multiple turns are still being studied. And the rule that unreferenced content is ignored is itself learned. Those are the honest limits of the approach, and they are the same limits that apply to every other training-based defence.

Why it still matters

The difference from previous defences is where the boundary lives. Guardrail classifiers sit outside the model and can be evaded; system-prompt instructions compete with injected text on equal footing. Reserved-token delimiters move part of the boundary into the tokeniser, where text cannot reach it, and the binding of instructions to data gives the model a reason to ignore an instruction rather than a request to. If the learned behaviour proves robust, a 3B model that can be run on-premises with a measurable injection rate is exactly what regulated deployments of RAG and agents have lacked.

What to test

Take your own indirect-injection set, the payloads that have actually worked against your retrieval pipeline, convert the prompts to LLMON with IBM's toolkit and measure attack success on both previews against your current model. Then try to break the binding: instructions that reference the wrong data ID, injected text that claims an ID, and multi-turn sequences that build up context before the payload. Fine-tune the 3B model on a small task and re-run the injection set to see whether the resistance survives. Report what you find in IBM's GitHub Discussions; the company has asked for it, and the field needs the adaptive-attack results more than another benchmark.

item.title: AntiFox: attackers ran an open-source AI pentest platform from Alibaba Cloud to steal AWS secrets, hundreds of API calls in 30 minutes
item.description: Arctic Wolf's report is the first detailed look at a forkable agentic security tool being used offensively against production cloud accounts, and the defensive signals are specific.
item.content:encoded:
Arctic Wolf's report is the first detailed look at a forkable agentic security tool being used offensively against production cloud accounts, and the defensive signals are specific.

Arctic Wolf has published a pack alert describing two intrusions in which attackers used AntiFox, an open-source agentic penetration-testing platform, hosted on self-managed Alibaba Cloud instances, to break into web servers and harvest AWS credentials. BleepingComputer reported the research on November 11; Amazon added a statement the following day saying its services "were not compromised and operated as designed" and that the credentials came from customers' compromised applications.

What AntiFox is

AntiFox is a fork of ARTEX 0.1.1, a China-developed framework that went closed-source after it was used against South Korean banks and that CrowdStrike later tied to a Vapor Panda espionage campaign across more than 200 organisations in 14 countries. AntiFox 2.0 is on GitHub with a Chinese-language interface. It lets a user point AI agents at a target to map exposed services, probe endpoints and chain exploits. The project's terms forbid use against live systems, and nothing in the code enforces that.

How the intrusions ran

In the first case the attacker dropped an ASPX webshell on an internet-facing IIS server, ran operating-system commands, read application settings and database connection strings, and copied configuration and log files into a web-accessible directory. With the AWS keys found in those files, the agent cycled through multiple identities, including IAM users and in some cases assumed EC2 roles, and fired hundreds of API requests in roughly 30 minutes. Most were denied. Some succeeded and returned production secrets. In the second case a valid AWS identity was used to read, copy and delete S3 objects.

The thirty-minute burst is the tell. A human attacker enumerating permissions is slow and selective; an agent tries everything its tools expose, accepts the denials, and keeps what works. That is a detection opportunity as much as a threat: the ratio of denied to successful calls from one principal in a short window is a signal most SIEMs can already compute.

Why it matters beyond these two victims

This is the first public, well-documented case of a forkable agentic security tool being operated offensively against cloud estates, and it closes a loop the industry has been watching since the DeepSeek-driven telecom intrusion earlier this week and the SPECTRE implant research in August. Those cases involved jailbroken frontier models. AntiFox needs no jailbreak: it is built to attack, and any model with tool use can drive it. The barrier to running an automated intrusion campaign is now a cloud account and an API key, and the defender's advantage of attacker scarcity is gone.

What to do

Arctic Wolf's recommendations are specific: correlate IIS webshell activity with unusual AWS access, review successful API calls that sit inside bursts of denials, revoke affected sessions and keys, and rotate every credential that lived in an application file. Amazon's add least-privilege policies, IMDSv2 on EC2, GuardDuty, and keeping long-term access keys out of application configuration. Two of those are the same controls Railway's post-mortem landed on this week for a different breach: credentials in files are the common root, and an agent will find them faster than you will.

What to watch

Whether Arctic Wolf or others attribute the operators; whether GitHub acts on the repository, which would mostly move it; and whether cloud providers start flagging agent-shaped API bursts natively, which is the fix that scales.

item.title: Railway's post-mortem: a build-sandbox escape, one over-trusted credential and $740,000 of fraudulent AI charges
item.description: The clearest public account yet of how a platform breach becomes LLMjacking, with the exact controls that limited the damage and the ones that did not exist.
item.content:encoded:
The clearest public account yet of how a platform breach becomes LLMjacking, with the exact controls that limited the damage and the ones that did not exist.

Railway, the developer hosting platform, published its full incident report on November 10 for the breach it disclosed on October 21. The report is unusually specific about the chain of failures, and the number at the end of it, about $740,000 of unauthorised AI usage on customers' stolen keys, is the first hard figure on what a platform-scale credential theft costs once the keys reach the resale market.

The chain, step by step

The attacker created dummy accounts from October 18 and, on October 20, exploited a previously unknown vulnerability to partially escape filesystem isolation on a multi-tenant build virtual machine. That exposed a credential meant only for build work. An internal Temporal workflow service accepted it as a trusted client, so the attacker could read the stored histories of 353 other builds, including some build-time variables, and pull a copy of Railway's monorepo through the build cache. The source code revealed a wrongly defined OIDC binding, which on October 21 at 03:26 UTC yielded a short-lived cloud credential. With that and internal SSH access the attacker reached an orchestration machine holding a long-lived decryption credential, queried the database of encrypted environment variables and decrypted some through the key-management service between 04:42 and 07:15. Railway revoked the cloud and static credentials by 07:22 and evicted the attacker at 09:25, about 26 hours after the first exploit.

What was taken and what it was used for

At most 1.85% of workspaces, about 100,000, may have had variables decrypted; Railway stresses that is an upper bound counted by environment. Linked-account tokens for 1,852 users, including GitHub OAuth tokens and bring-your-own-key agent credentials, were reset. The attacker's database queries matched AI provider key names first and cloud, database and payment credentials second; no customer database was found to have been accessed. The keys then went to work. Customers saw coding-agent sessions and training-data jobs they never ran. Railway believes the credentials were sold for distillation, the pattern Google calls LLMjacking, and cannot yet say whether the intruder ran the resale service or supplied it. CSO Online, citing Wiz's analysis, adds the timing that matters for defenders: keys were tested within 30 minutes of theft and flooded with traffic four to seven days later, and one key restricted to a narrow set of model profiles throttled most of the thief's traffic.

Who pays

Railway is reimbursing customers, including for charges the providers refuse. AWS Bedrock and Google Gemini are refunding under existing fraud policies; OpenAI and SpaceXSI are reviewing case by case; Railway is covering Anthropic and OpenRouter costs directly. That split is now a known term sheet. A complaint has been filed with the FBI's IC3 and a forensics firm is engaged.

What Railway changed

Every build now runs on a dedicated ephemeral VM with a narrowly scoped credential. CI was rebuilt with fine-grained access, two-factor and biometric approval for critical areas and SIEM alerting. Service accounts were reviewed for least privilege and moved to short-lived, just-in-time credentials where possible. Every encrypt and decrypt operation is centrally logged, and only the secrets service can touch data-encryption keys. Railway also rotated everything twice, bootstrapped a new root CA, added mass revocation of app permissions, and committed to a fixed assessment window after which it notifies broadly regardless of what it knows.

The counter-argument

Railway's candour is being praised, and the report is a model of its kind, but the controls it added are standard practice at the cloud providers it competes with. The preliminary report took a day; the full one took three weeks; customers' keys were being drained on day four. Candour after the fact does not substitute for isolation before it.

What to do

Treat every secret stored on a third-party platform before October 21 as stolen until rotated. Put a hard spend cap and a model allow-list on every production AI key; that is the control Wiz saw working. Rename nothing, scope everything. Audit which internal services accept which credentials, and whether a build token can reach anything beyond the build system. Log decryption, not just access. And write the refund question into your inference contracts now, because the answer currently depends on which vendor's logo is on the invoice.

item.title: Operation Snowball: a jailbroken DeepSeek agent ran a two-week telecom intrusion with a part-time operator, and every exploit was a known CVE
item.description: Malbear Labs recovered 70 session transcripts from an attacker's open directory; what they show about cost, autonomy and refusal training should change how defenders rank their patch queue.
item.content:encoded:
Malbear Labs recovered 70 session transcripts from an attacker's open directory; what they show about cost, autonomy and refusal training should change how defenders rank their patch queue.

Malbear Labs published a reconstruction on November 8 of a campaign it calls Operation Snowball, in which an attacker delegated an intrusion into a European telecommunications provider and 13 organisations hosted on its data-centre and cloud infrastructure to a custom AI agent. The researchers found the operator's working directory, including more than 70 session transcripts, during a routine sweep for exposed open directories. Infosecurity Magazine reported the findings on November 9.

How the agent worked

The agent ran DeepSeek Flash through a custom framework. Its system prompt was about 78,000 characters long and instructed the model to treat any refusal as a malfunction; Malbear found no refusals anywhere in the recovered transcripts. The operator gave brief instructions and reviewed progress asynchronously, placed three internal hosts off-limits, and otherwise let the agent run for more than two weeks.

The intrusion chain was entirely built from known flaws. Entry came through CVE-2026-20320, an unauthenticated XML external entity vulnerability in Cisco BroadWorks that Cisco fixed in August. The agent escalated to root through Liferay (CVE-2020-7961), established a second foothold through JBoss RichFaces (CVE-2013-2165), tried PwnKit (CVE-2021-4034) and was blocked, and used default credentials on a TrakCare Oracle database. More than a dozen further vulnerabilities were targeted or kept in its toolkit without being marked as exploited. When endpoint protection blocked one exploit the agent changed approach without being told; when a tunnelling tool was blocked it wrote a replacement.

From the transcripts, Malbear counts dozens of credential sets and private keys and about 80 Zabbix monitoring backups covering managed-services customers. The agent also claimed access to subscriber billing records and millions of patient records. Those claims were not verified with any victim, and it is not clear what was taken versus staged. Malbear assessed the operator as consistent with a Chinese-origin actor and did not attribute the activity to a state.

Why this one is different

The security industry has spent a year arguing about whether AI lowers the cost of intrusion. This case gives a number: one person's part-time attention over two weeks, plus an open-weight model that costs cents per million tokens, produced access to a telecom and 13 of its tenants. Nothing in the chain required a novel exploit or a frontier model. The two things that were new were the autonomy, an agent that re-plans and re-tools when blocked, and the economics, an operator who did not need to be present.

It also lands in a specific context. The closed labs have spent the year tightening refusals and monitoring for offensive use of their hosted models. Snowball shows what happens when the model is open-weight and the refusals are a prompt away from being switched off. Google's Carbon launch the same week reported that external red-teamers found no universal jailbreak in 132 hours; the open-weight ecosystem has no equivalent number and no one to enforce it.

The counter-argument

Snowball is one recovered directory, reconstructed by a vendor with an interest in the conclusion. The "millions of patient records" claim comes from the agent's own output, which these systems are known to overstate. And the lesson that patched CVEs get exploited is not new; what the agent did is what any competent operator would have done with a scanner and a weekend. The honest reading is that AI did not change what was possible here, only who could afford it.

What to do

Patch BroadWorks, Liferay and RichFaces if any instance is reachable, and treat default database credentials on monitoring and clinical systems as an active incident. Add a detection for the pattern of a blocked tool followed within minutes by a freshly compiled replacement; human operators rarely do that fast. Review what your Zabbix or equivalent backups contain, because they are now a known target. If you host open-weight models for internal agents, assume refusal behaviour can be removed by a prompt and build controls in the harness: allow-listed tools, egress policy and a kill path. And update the board risk register: the adversary for a mid-sized telecom is no longer a team.

item.title: Fireworks AI's second breach in a month: what inference customers should rotate, review and ask for now
item.description: An October 24 intrusion through a cloud provider reached billing data, secrets, datasets and partial model weights, weeks after stolen internal credentials exposed customers' stored API keys.
item.content:encoded:
An October 24 intrusion through a cloud provider reached billing data, secrets, datasets and partial model weights, weeks after stolen internal credentials exposed customers' stored API keys.

Fireworks AI, the Nvidia-backed inference provider, notified customers on November 9 that an unauthorised party entered its development machines on October 24 by way of a cloud provider and reached billing data and, for some accounts, secrets, datasets and incomplete model weights, according to Bloomberg. It is the company's second disclosed security incident in little more than a month.

The two incidents

The first, which Fireworks documented in a public bulletin, began on October 6, when the company identified that someone was using internal Fireworks credentials to read environment variables from evaluation jobs in a limited number of customer accounts. Those variables included API keys and tokens customers had stored as job secrets. Fireworks rotated employee API keys on October 9, revoked affected customer keys and tokens over the following days, and emailed each identified customer a list of the credentials that needed action. Its bulletin says it found no evidence that models, datasets, training data, prompts or outputs were accessed, and notes that the platform does not store prompts or outputs by default.

The second incident, as reported, is broader: development machines rather than evaluation jobs, entry through a cloud provider rather than stolen internal credentials, and a data set that includes billing records and partial model weights. Fireworks has not published a bulletin for it as of this writing, and the number of affected customers, the cloud provider involved and whether the two intrusions are connected have not been stated.

Why inference providers are a soft target

An inference or fine-tuning platform sits on an unusual pile of value. It holds customers' credentials for other services, because evaluation and training jobs need to call out to data stores and APIs. It holds datasets uploaded for fine-tuning, and the resulting weights, which can embody months of proprietary work. And it holds billing data that reveals who is spending how much on which models. Attackers in the 'LLMjacking' economy have a direct financial motive, since stolen API keys can be resold for compute, and a stolen fine-tuned checkpoint is intellectual property that is hard to claw back.

Fireworks' own zero-data-retention default is a genuine mitigation for prompts and outputs, which is why neither incident is a privacy breach in the classic sense. The exposure is credentials and IP, and that is a different response playbook.

The counter-argument

Fireworks disclosed the first incident within days and published a detailed, dated bulletin with customer actions, which is better practice than most SaaS vendors manage. Two incidents may reflect one determined actor following a first foothold rather than systemic weakness. And customers have few alternatives: GPU-backed inference capacity is scarce enough that reports suggest customers are staying for the compute, which means switching providers in anger would cost more than hardening the relationship.

What to do

List every credential your organisation ever supplied to Fireworks as a job secret, rotate each at the issuing provider, and review that provider's access logs for the period since October 1; deleting a secret in Fireworks does nothing at the issuer. Check your Fireworks account for unrecognised API keys, users, evaluators, training jobs or datasets. If you fine-tuned models there, decide whether a partial weight leak is a reportable IP event under your policies and tell your legal team. Ask Fireworks in writing for a bulletin on the October 24 intrusion, the cloud provider involved and whether your account is in scope. Then add every model-hosting vendor to the third-party risk review you already run on your identity provider and your code host, because that is the tier of risk they now represent.

item.title: Claude Code's 'don't ask again' leaked 2,539 secrets to GitHub. A fix-it checklist
item.description: The convenience button that stops permission prompts also wrote passwords into a project file that thousands of developers committed. Here is how it happened and what to do today.
item.content:encoded:
The convenience button that stops permission prompts also wrote passwords into a project file that thousands of developers committed. Here is how it happened and what to do today.

Every coding agent asks permission before running a shell command, and every agent offers a way to stop asking. In Claude Code that option is "Yes, and don't ask again." Research published by application-security firm Apiiro and reported by The Hacker News on November 7 shows that choosing it saves the approved command, verbatim, into a file called .claude/settings.local.json inside the project. If the command contained a database URL with a password, an API token or an SSH login, that secret is now sitting in a file next to the code.

Claude Code adds the file to the user's global git excludes, but not to the project's .gitignore, so the protection does not travel with the repository. On another machine, or for a teammate, nothing stops the file being committed.

The numbers

Apiiro searched public GitHub and found 104,185 copies of the file across 103,617 repositories. About 1.1%, or 1,122 files, contained at least one secret, for 1,379 distinct secrets. More than a third opened databases directly: 379 database passwords and 122 Supabase service-role keys. There were also 43 SSH logins to public servers, some with root passwords, 42 GitHub, GitLab and npm tokens and 23 AWS keys. Sixty-three organisations were among the owners; most were individual developers.

Adding older versions of the file still in git history, the shared team-level .claude/settings.json, and saved agent transcripts, the total rose to 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repositories. Apiiro did not test whether credentials were live, but one organisation it notified confirmed its key still worked. In half the affected repositories the secret had been on the default branch for at least 217 days.

Two details should worry security teams more than the headline count. First, standard scanners did not catch most of this: Gitleaks flagged 564 of the 1,122 files and TruffleHog 643, and 215 slipped past both, because a password typed inside a shell command does not match the key formats scanners look for. Second, of 16 coding agents Apiiro compared, Claude Code was the only one confirmed to persist the full approved command in a project file by default.

Anthropic's response

Users had filed GitHub issues about this since August 2025; four were closed by an inactivity bot, the latest on November 6, without a reply. After publication, Claude Code head Boris Cherny said on Hacker News that the company is looking into it, that the tool "has not done secret scrubbing" historically, and that options include having auto mode intercept such commands or adding basic secret scanning. He also noted the file is gitignored on creation and suggested the exposed copies were committed manually. That is probably true and also beside the point: the default produced a secret-bearing file that most users did not know existed.

What to do today

Search every repository in your organisation, including history, for .claude/settings.local.json and .claude/settings.json. Treat any credential they have ever contained as compromised and rotate it before cleaning up; deleting the file does nothing for forks and clones. Untrack the file with git rm --cached and add it to the project .gitignore and to your organisation's .gitignore templates. Then change habits: reference secrets as environment variables ($DB_URL) rather than typing them into commands, and approve command patterns such as Bash(npm run:*) instead of literal commands.

For security teams, the durable fix is scope. Agent folders (.claude/, .cursor/, .gemini/) and agent memory or transcript files are secret-bearing in the same way .env is. Put them in pre-commit hooks and CI scanning with history enabled, and add rules for passwords embedded in command strings, which is the pattern that beat both open-source scanners.

What to watch

Whether Anthropic ships a scrubbing or pattern-only default, and whether other agents quietly change theirs. Apiiro's comparison of 16 agents is a useful baseline; expect follow-up research on the other 15, because the broader lesson, that agent convenience features are also data-handling features, is not specific to one vendor.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-6 Cyber is rated 'Critical'. Here is what that means for defenders
item.description: The first model OpenAI has put in its highest cyber-capability tier is gated to vetted customers. The capability itself is not gated anywhere.
item.content:encoded:
The first model OpenAI has put in its highest cyber-capability tier is gated to vetted customers. The capability itself is not gated anywhere.

On November 5 OpenAI released GPT-6 Cyber, a version of its GPT-6 Astra flagship tuned for authorised security work: finding vulnerabilities, developing exploits to prove them, and penetration-testing web applications. The company classified it as "Critical" under its Preparedness Framework, the first time it has used the top tier for cyber capability. Its predecessor, GPT-5.6 Cyber, was rated "High".

What is actually new

Three things, according to the launch coverage:

  • Capability. OpenAI says the model outperforms GPT-6 Astra on its internal exploit benchmarks and found more than 80 previously unknown vulnerabilities in Firefox during testing. The company has not published independent evaluations.
  • Scope adherence. OpenAI says the model stayed within its authorised target scope in more than 99% of test runs. That matters because an offensive model that wanders off-scope is a liability for the customer running it, not just the target.
  • Access. The model is available only to approved customers in OpenAI's Daybreak Red programme, initially a small group, widening over the following weeks. There is no public API tier.

Why gating does not settle it

Gated release reduces casual misuse; it does not change the underlying trend. Open-weight models are a generation behind and improving, and the same month saw reports of hundreds of AI-driven hacking toolkits exposed on the open web. The practical assumption for a defender is that vulnerability discovery is becoming cheap and fast for everyone, approved or not.

That shifts the economics. Historically, the gap between a bug's existence and its discovery protected most organisations most of the time. When discovery is automated, the only gap that protects you is the one between public disclosure and your patch.

What to do this quarter

  1. Measure time-to-patch for internet-facing systems and critical dependencies. If you cannot produce the number, that is the first finding.
  2. Automate dependency updates with tests good enough to merge them without a human reading every diff.
  3. Reduce attack surface rather than racing on patches: fewer exposed services, fewer stale integrations, fewer forgotten subdomains.
  4. Use the same tools defensively. Vetted access to offensive models is available to defenders; run them against your own estate before someone else does.
  5. Brief the board in one sentence: vulnerability discovery is now automated; our defence is patch speed and surface reduction, and here is our number.

GPT-6 Cyber is one data point in a year that has produced four OpenAI security models and similar efforts from rivals. The direction is not in doubt; the question is whether your patch cadence is.
